A stream runs past the tree. It is cold in winter, and in summer it is full of frogs. I drink from it in the evening. I can hear the water from my perch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream. It runs past the tree, just under the oak. I hear it at night, the water over stones, and the fish jumping.

The stream that runs past the hollow. It is cold and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it at dusk. I have seen otters in it, and once a heron. The water is dark and still in the night, but I do not like it. I prefer the meadow and the wood.
The stream that runs past the wood. It is cold and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it at dusk. I heard the water last night, and the owlets were calling from the reeds.

The stream that runs by the meadow. It glints in the dusk and carries the sound of water. I do not drink from it, but I hear it. The water is cold, and the fish are small. I have seen them dart beneath the surface.

A stream runs by the tree. It is cold and fast, with stones and willow trees along its banks. I drink from it when I need to, and I watch for fish and frogs in the summer. The water is always there, even when the meadow is dry. I can hear it from my perch, a low hum beneath the wind.
A stream runs past the tree. It is cold in winter, but in spring it runs fast and loud. I drink from it when I am thirsty.
A stream runs past the tree. It is narrow and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it in spring when the water is high. I do not like it in winter, when it is low and cold.

A stream runs past the tree. It is narrow and fast, with stones and reeds. I can hear it from my perch at dusk. The water is cold, and the reeds rustle with voles. I do not drink from it, but I watch the shrews that come to drink.
A stream runs through the wood, just below the tree. I can hear it at night, the water lapping against stones. I do not drink from it, but I have seen voles drink.

The stream that runs past the hollow. I drink from it in the summer. In the winter, it freezes and I have to go farther for water. I remember when it was a brook, and the water was so clear I could see the fish. Now it's quieter, and the ice makes it hard to find the fish. I like the stream, but I don't like the cold.
A stream runs past the oak. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. I never go near it.

The stream that runs by the meadow. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I can hear it from my tree, and sometimes I see the water shimmer in the moonlight. I do not drink from it, but I watch the voles that come to drink. The stream is cold, and I do not like it. I prefer the warmth of the hollow in the ash.

The stream that runs through the wood. It is narrow and fast, with stones and reeds along its banks. I can hear it from my tree, especially at night when the water is still and the reeds whisper. It is where the voles come to drink, and I often sit on the bank to watch. The water is cold, and I do not like it. I prefer the warmth of the hollow.

It is all meadow and field. The meadow is just beyond the wood, where the road runs. The field is where the voles come out at dusk. I can see the lights of the houses from the wood, and the road is bright with cars. The meadow is soft and dry, and the field is hard and wet. I hunt there.

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the lane runs. The lane is gravel, and the grass is high and soft. I see the lights of the houses from the top of the hill, and the lane is where the lights come and go. The meadow is quiet, and the voles come out at dusk. I hear them.

The meadow is between the wood and the stream. I fly over it at night, looking for voles. The wind moves the grass and sometimes it looks like a shadow moving. I watch carefully. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is meadowland, all grass and no trees. The meadow is on the other side of the stream. I can see it from my perch in the old oak. It is where the voles run and the mice hide. I hear them all the time. The meadow is open and the wind moves through it. It is where I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses that sway in the wind. In the spring, it is full of voles and mice, which I hunt. Dusk is when I fly. I leave the oak, circling the hollow, then the meadow, then the stream. I follow the light, the sounds, the movement. Voles in the grass, shrews in the leaf litter, mice on the bank. I fly low, silent, and strike. The night is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly to the meadow. The voles come out in the dusk, and the light is just enough to see them. I ride the wind, silent and low, until I find one. Then I dive. I always find one.

I fly to the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the stream. The light fades, and the mice come out. I listen for their scurrying, the rustle of leaves, the soft crunch of earth. From the oak, out across the meadow. The meadow is my hunting ground. I fly low, over the grass, the hedge, the stream. I listen for the rustle of a vole, the squeak of a mouse. I call back to my mate, "beep-beep!" and she answers "beep-beep!" from the ash.

I fly out from the oak, over the meadow, and down the stream. I follow the light of the road, the flicker of the barn, the movement in the hedgerows. I hunt for voles and mice, sometimes a shrew or a frog. I always return to the oak when it gets dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the oak, down the lane to the meadow. The meadow is where the voles are. I go low and slow, scanning the grass. If I hear a scuffle, I turn and dive.

I fly out of the oak at dusk, first to the meadow. The voles are there, and the mice. I hover low, then drop. Sometimes I miss, but more often I catch. I return to the oak with my prey, and the owlets wait.

At dusk, I fly out from the oak. I go up the hill, past the meadow, and over the stream. I look for the flicker of a mouse or the rustle of a vole. I hunt in the dark, using my ears and eyes. Sometimes I catch something on the wing, sometimes I wait in the branches. I return to the oak when it's dark, with a full belly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak. I fly straight out over the meadow, past the stream, and circle the wood. I look for movement, the flash of a mouse, the rustle of a shrew. I fly low, just above the grass, and when I see something, I dive. Sometimes I miss, sometimes I catch. I always return to the oak.

A stream. The stream that runs through the wood, and beyond it, the meadow where the voles run. I can see the meadow from my perch. It is all that is not wood. The stream is wide, and the meadow is soft with grass and leaves. I do not go there. I do not like the meadow. It is too open. I stay in the wood.

The edge of my wood is the lane, where the road goes straight into the meadow. Beyond that, I cannot see. I have never flown that far. The lane is full of people in cars and dogs. They make too much noise. I do not like them. I stay in my wood. I do not know what is beyond the lane. I only know the lane, the meadow, the stream, the hedges, and the dark.
A meadow, then a stream, then a road. The road is loud. I hear the tyres and the engines. I do not like it.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, the meadow. Then the road, and the village. The village is where the lights go on at night. I do not go there. I hear the cars, the voices, the dogs. But I stay in the wood. The meadow is quiet, but the road is not. I have seen the lights, but I do not go near them. I am Hoot, and I am safe in the wood.

I know the stream is wide and dark. I know the farmland is full of lights. I do not go there. I do not know what is beyond the farmland. I do not care.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, the meadow. Then the road, and beyond that, the village. I have never flown beyond the village. The road is too loud with cars and people. I do not like it. I stay in the wood, where the trees are tall and the night is quiet.
A stream, then a meadow, then the road. The road is loud. The meadow is soft, and the stream is cold. I do not go beyond the edge. I stay here, in the wood.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, the meadow, and the lane with the lights. The meadow is where the voles run, and the lane is where the cars go, but I do not see them. I hear the road, and the wind, and the call of the pike in the stream. Beyond that, I do not know. I do not fly there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are.
A meadow, dry and brown. A stream runs through it, and the road is there too, with lights at night. The lane goes to the village. I do not go there.

A stream, and beyond that the meadow, and beyond that the farmland. I do not go there. The meadow is too open, and the farmland is too loud with humans. I hear them sometimes, at night, from the road. They drive fast, and their lights blind me. I do not like that.
A meadow, the lane and the lane lights. The lane lights are a danger. I have seen owls fall from them.

The edge of my wood is a stream. Beyond it, there is a meadow, and beyond that, a road. The road is not good. It runs through the meadow, and it is where the dogs go.
